artists.biography:
The Pogues are a Celtic punk band from London, formed in 1982 and fronted by Shane MacGowan. The band reached international prominence in the 1980s and early 1990s. MacGowan left the band in 1991 due to drinking problems but the band continued first with Joe Strummer and then with Spider Stacy on vocals before breaking up in 1996. The band reformed in 2001, and has been playing regularly ever since, most notably on the US East Coast around St Patrick's Day and across the UK and Ireland every December. The group has yet to record any new music and, according to Spider Stacy on Pogues.com, has no inclination to do so.
Their politically tinged music was informed by MacGowan and Stacy's punk backgrounds, yet used traditional Irish instruments such as the tin whistle, cittern, mandolin and accordion.
The Pogues were founded in Kings Cross, a district of Central London, in 1982 as Pogue Mahone—pogue mahone being the Anglicisation of the Irish póg mo thóin, meaning "kiss my arse".

perplexity.description:
The Rest of the Best by The Pogues, originally released in 1992, is a compilation album that gathers some of the band's most notable tracks not included on their earlier Best Of collection. Musically, the album showcases the band's signature blend of punk rock energy and traditional Irish folk, featuring instruments like tin whistle, banjo, and accordion alongside driving rock rhythms. The songs range from raucous anthems to poignant ballads, reflecting the group's knack for combining rowdy pub singalongs with politically charged storytelling.

This release serves as a companion to the band's 1991 Best Of compilation, rounding out their most popular material from the 1980s and early 1990s. It captures The Pogues at the height of their influence, shortly after the departure of frontman Shane MacGowan, and includes fan favorites such as "If I Should Fall from Grace with God," "Boys from the County Hell," and their cover of "Honky Tonk Women." While not a studio album, The Rest of the Best is an essential part of the band's discography, offering a comprehensive look at their eclectic style and lasting impact on the Celtic punk genre.

Critically, the album was well received as a solid representation of The Pogues' unique sound and legacy. It performed respectably commercially, further cementing the band's reputation as pioneers who bridged the gap between punk and traditional Irish music. The compilation remains a key entry for both longtime fans and newcomers seeking to explore the breadth of The Pogues' influential catalog.
